opus-5.5.text:
So, the way I like to think about it is that data like images or text are not just a cloud of points in a high-dimensional space. They have structure, and a very important part of that structure is that it's hierarchical and compositional. A sentence is made of phrases, phrases are made of words, words of letters. An image of a dog is made of a head and a body, the head of eyes and ears, and so on down to edges and textures. The question is how a network trained on finitely many examples can discover these levels of representation, and why it needs a certain amount of data to do so.

To make this concrete, we've worked with simple generative models of data, which we call random hierarchy models. You can think of them as a kind of probabilistic grammar. You start with a high-level label, the class, and it gets rewritten into a tuple of lower-level features, which are rewritten again, until you reach the visible input. A key ingredient is that there are many equivalent ways to rewrite a feature, which you can think of as synonyms. Two different low-level patterns can mean the same thing at the next level up. To classify well, the network has to learn that these synonyms are equivalent, that is, become invariant to exchanging them. That invariance is what an abstract representation is.

How does it learn that from data? The answer we found is through correlations. Synonymous low-level patterns have the same correlations with the label, or with other parts of the input. If two groups of pixels or two sequences of words show up in the same contexts and predict the same things, the network can infer that they play the same role. But these correlations are weak and only become detectable once you have enough samples to beat the sampling noise. That gives a characteristic number of training examples for each level of the hierarchy. You can estimate it, and it matches quite well what we observe when we train deep networks on this data.

What comes out of this picture is that abstraction emerges in steps. With little data, the network can only resolve correlations over short distances, local structure, so it builds low-level representations. As you add data, longer-range correlations become statistically resolvable, and the network can group things at the next level and build more abstract representations. It's a ladder: each rung of abstraction is unlocked when the data is sufficient to detect the corresponding correlations.

We've seen the same thing in a more realistic setting with language models trained on next-token prediction. The range of context a model effectively uses grows with the training set, and as it grows, the model captures deeper levels of the latent structure. This connects to scaling laws. The smooth power-law improvement in loss may result from the model successively learning these levels, each contributing a small piece of the improvement.

One more point I find important is that this also explains why deep, hierarchical architectures help. If your architecture can represent the data's hierarchical structure, and if invariance to synonyms is built up layer by layer, the number of samples you need can become polynomial in the dimension instead of exponential. That's a way of understanding how these networks beat the curse of dimensionality. They aren't learning arbitrary functions in high dimension. They exploit the fact that the world is compositional, and they discover that composition from the statistics of the data, one level of abstraction at a time.

r001.rationale: It says abstraction emerges in steps as more data makes longer-range correlations detectable, enabling successively higher-level representations.

r002.rationale: It describes networks learning more abstract representations with more data, but does not state that the network is very large.

r003.rationale: It describes abstraction levels becoming available as data grows, but does not clearly identify the most abstract concepts as the hardest to learn.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, that's really the central question I've been obsessed with for the last few years. And I think the honest answer is that we don't have a complete theory, but we're starting to get a picture, and the picture is tied to the structure of the data itself.

So let me step back. The classical view in statistical learning theory is that learning in high dimensions should be essentially impossible. If you think of a function on, say, a million-dimensional input space, and you make no assumptions about it, the number of samples you need to learn it grows exponentially with the dimension. That's the curse of dimensionality. And yet deep networks learn images, learn language, with a number of examples that is, by comparison, tiny. So something about the structure of real data has to be making the problem tractable, and the question is what.

The hypothesis that I find most compelling, and which we've been trying to formalize, is that natural data is hierarchical and compositional. An image is made of objects, objects are made of parts, parts are made of edges and textures, and so on down to pixels. A sentence is made of clauses, clauses of phrases, phrases of words. And crucially, the lower-level features are reused. The same kind of edge appears in a cat and a car. The same word appears in very different sentences. This reuse is what a deep network can exploit.

To study this, we've built synthetic models of data, generative models we call the random hierarchy model, where you have a class label at the top, and that label generates a few high-level features according to some rules, and each of those generates lower-level features, and so on, down to the actual input. It's essentially a probabilistic context-free grammar. What's nice is that this is simple enough that you can compute things, and yet it has the two ingredients I mentioned, hierarchy and compositionality.

What we find is something I think is quite beautiful. There's a well-defined sample complexity, a number of training examples at which the network suddenly learns the task. And this number is polynomial in the input dimension, not exponential. So the hierarchy does break the curse. But the mechanism by which it does this is the interesting part, and it connects directly to your question.

The network cannot learn the top-level class directly from the pixels. There are too many possible configurations. What it does instead is learn correlations. The lowest-level features, the little groups of pixels, are correlated with the label. Not strongly, but a little. If you have enough data, you can detect that correlation, and once you detect it, the network effectively groups together all the low-level patterns that have the same statistical relationship to the output. It's building a representation that is invariant to which specific synonym was used, if you like. And that representation is now a lower-dimensional, more abstract object. And then it can play the same game one level up. The correlations between these new abstract features and the label are easier to detect, and so on.

So the emergence of abstraction, in this view, is really the emergence of invariances. The network learns to ignore the details that don't matter for prediction, level by level, and what remains is the concept. And the point at which it becomes able to do this is set by when the data is sufficient to resolve the relevant correlations against the noise. That's why it depends on data in this quite sharp way.

And I'll say one thing that surprised us. When you look at the learning dynamics in time, you see that the network learns these levels in a sequence. Low-level structure first, then progressively higher. It's not that everything gets refined simultaneously. There are stages. And in the language models setting, which we've looked at more recently with similar synthetic grammars, you see the same thing. The model first captures things like which tokens co-occur, then phrase-like structure, then longer-range dependencies. The effective context length it uses grows as training proceeds. Each stage corresponds to resolving another level of the hierarchy.

Now, I want to be honest about the limitations. These are toy models. Real data isn't generated by a clean context-free grammar. But I think the value of a toy model in physics has always been that it isolates a mechanism, and then you check whether the mechanism's fingerprints show up in the real system. And some of them do. The sample complexity scaling, the staged dynamics, the fact that intermediate layers of real networks do become increasingly invariant to irrelevant transformations with depth. These are all consistent with the picture.

So if I had to summarize, I'd say abstraction emerges because the data is built out of reusable parts, and the network discovers those parts by detecting statistical regularities, which requires a certain amount of data at each level. More data lets you resolve finer correlations, which lets you build the next level of the hierarchy. That's the mechanism as I currently understand it.

r001.rationale: It says the network learns levels in sequence as training proceeds, progressing from low-level structure to higher levels, and that more data enables each next level.

r002.rationale: The response discusses deep networks and increasing abstraction with more data, but does not state that the network is very large.

r003.rationale: It describes learning progressively higher levels, but does not identify the most abstract concepts as the hardest to learn; it says correlations at higher levels are easier to detect.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is what we mean by an abstract concept. One way to think about it is that there are many variations in the input that do not matter for the task. If you recognize an object, for example, its position or the background can change without changing what it is. An abstract representation would retain what matters while becoming insensitive to those other variations.

Then the question is: how does learning discover that structure? With a small amount of data, there may be many ways to fit the examples, including ways that depend on accidental correlations. As you get more data, those correlations become less useful, and features that are shared across examples can become more useful. But this also depends on the architecture and on the learning dynamics. More data alone is not an explanation.

From a physics perspective, what I find interesting is whether this happens progressively or whether there are relatively sharp changes, where a new feature becomes learnable and the representation reorganizes. You can study that in simplified models. The challenge is then to establish whether the same mechanisms explain the emergence of richer concepts in realistic networks. I would distinguish that question from simply observing that performance improves with training.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether emergence is progressive or involves sharp changes; it does not state that abstractions emerge progressively with training.

r002.rationale: It discusses how more data can make shared features more useful, but does not say that a very large neural network learns increasingly abstract concepts as it receives more data.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify the most abstract concepts as the hardest for neural networks to learn.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is what we mean by an abstract concept. One possibility is that the network learns a representation that keeps what is relevant to a task while becoming insensitive to details that are not relevant. Different inputs can then be treated as equivalent, even though they look quite different at the level of pixels, for example.

But saying that this happens because we have more data and more training is not yet an explanation. We would like to understand the mechanism: which features are learned first, what determines whether a useful feature can be discovered, and how that depends on the architecture and the structure of the data.

You can imagine that a simple statistical regularity is accessible early in training, whereas another regularity only becomes accessible once the representation has changed. Learning one feature can make learning another feature easier. That gives you a possible route toward increasingly abstract representations, but it is something we need to establish in models where we can actually follow the dynamics.

So I would distinguish the observation that representations become more useful or more invariant from a theory of why they do. The interesting challenge is to turn that observation into quantitative predictions about when a new feature will emerge and how much data it will require.

r001.rationale: The response describes a possible route to increasingly abstract representations, but says it needs to be established; it does not state that abstractions do emerge progressively with more training.

r002.rationale: It mentions more data but does not say that a very large network learns increasingly abstract concepts as it receives more data.

r003.rationale: It does not identify the most abstract concepts as the hardest for neural networks to learn.
